strengths: The work addresses an important evaluation gap: visual geometry capabilities beyond semantic recognition and simple positional relations. VGBench contributes 6,000 questions covering camera parameters, relative pose, homographies, depth, and correspondence, with clear relevance to computer vision.

SpatialScore provides substantial evaluation breadth: 28,093 samples from 12 sources, multiple input modalities and answer formats, and evaluations of 25 open models. The category-level and source-level results provide useful diagnostic information beyond a single leaderboard score.

SpatialAgent demonstrates substantial practical gains on SpatialScore-Hard. For example, the InternVL3-8B-based Plan-Execute system achieves 46.08% compared with 12.86% for its base model, supporting the usefulness of integrating specialist perception tools.

The supplementary material provides extensive question templates, agent prompts, tool interfaces, decoding settings, and dataset statistics. These details improve transparency and provide a meaningful foundation for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central concern is the validity of some geometry questions as measures of visual understanding. Appendix D.2 requests 3D boxes in world coordinates without specifying the world reference frame or supplying camera extrinsics. Such coordinates cannot generally be recovered from an RGB image alone. Figure 7 also asks a model to distinguish focal lengths of 792.59 and 792.95 pixels from a single ordinary scene image, without calibration information. These examples conflate genuine reasoning difficulty with unavailable information or unjustified precision, weakening the interpretation of low accuracy.

The claimed quality of distractors is not adequately validated. Figure 2 includes negative box dimensions in two distractors despite specifying the format as position plus size, creating an answer-elimination shortcut. Appendix D.2 generates incorrect distance options within ±50% of the ground truth, even though the open-ended scoring accepts answers between 0.5 and 2 times the ground truth. Thus, every such distractor would be acceptable under the open-ended criterion. The benchmark lacks text-only controls, quantitative ambiguity audits, and threshold sensitivity analysis to establish what its aggregate score measures.

SpatialScore-Hard is selected using failures of the same model families subsequently compared on it, including the agent backbones. This is reasonable for stress testing, but their low scores are partly a consequence of selection, and comparisons with systems outside the selection pool require qualification. SpatialAgent is evaluated only on this subset; results on the full benchmark or an independently selected subset are needed to support its broader superiority claims.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of the proposed agent architecture. Plan-Execute and ReAct combine existing orchestration patterns with existing expert models, but there are no tool ablations, direct specialist-tool baselines, or matched-budget reasoning controls. Appendix D.3 gives agents longer outputs and repeated interactions than ordinary baselines. Consequently, the gains establish the value of the overall tool-assisted system, but not the claimed novelty or specific advantage of multi-agent coordination. Runtime and tool-call costs are also unreported.

Dataset validation remains insufficiently documented for a benchmark contribution: manual checking lacks an annotator protocol, agreement statistics, or measured error rates, and the point-correspondence construction does not describe visibility or occlusion checks. No human-performance study supports the introduction's claim that models lag behind humans. Although the extensive implementation descriptions are valuable, code and data availability is only promised. These concerns are secondary to the question-validity and comparison issues, which determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a relevant computer vision problem: evaluating geometric perception beyond semantic recognition. VGBench contributes 6,000 questions derived from annotated 3D scenes, including camera pose, homography, depth, and correspondence tasks.

SpatialScore provides substantial evaluation breadth: 28,093 questions across 12 sources, eight task categories, multiple input modalities, and three answer formats. The evaluation of 25 models and detailed per-dataset results are useful empirical contributions.

SpatialAgent demonstrates promising practical gains. On SpatialScore-Hard, the Qwen-based Plan-Execute system reaches 35.30% versus 15.21% for its backbone, while the Intern-based system reaches 46.08%. These results support the usefulness of combining MLLMs with specialist vision tools.

The supplement provides extensive question templates, prompts, tool interfaces, and inference settings, improving reproducibility. Reporting both successful and failed agent trajectories also helps expose practical limitations.
weaknesses: The principal concern is benchmark validity. Appendix D.2 asks for 3D boxes in world coordinates without specifying an observable world reference frame. Figure 7 asks a single RGB image to distinguish focal lengths of 792.59 and 792.95 pixels. Absolute world coordinates and such precise calibration are not generally identifiable from these inputs. Consequently, some errors may reflect missing information rather than deficient spatial reasoning. No human study or task-level answerability audit establishes the claimed human–model gap.

Distractor quality is insufficiently validated. Figure 2 includes negative size components in two distractor 3D boxes, allowing elimination without inspecting the image. Appendix D.2 also generates distance distractors within ±50% of ground truth, although the open-ended scoring rule accepts answers within a factor of two. Thus, values treated as wrong in multiple-choice questions can qualify as correct in open-ended questions. No text-only baseline or format-sensitivity analysis quantifies these effects.

SpatialScore-Hard is selected using failures of models subsequently evaluated on it, including the agent backbones. This is useful for targeted diagnosis, but systematically disadvantages the selection models when comparing them with excluded models and tool-augmented systems. SpatialAgent is evaluated quantitatively only on this subset; an independently selected test set or full-benchmark evaluation is needed to substantiate general superiority.

The agent experiments do not isolate the contribution of the proposed orchestration. There are no tool-removal ablations, direct specialist-tool baselines, or matched-budget reasoning controls. Appendix D.3 permits agents longer outputs and repeated interactions, while ordinary baselines typically receive 512 tokens. The gains establish the value of the complete system, but do not establish that its multi-agent structure is necessary or novel beyond standard Plan-Execute and ReAct workflows. Runtime and tool-call costs are also unreported.

The unified score obscures important evaluation differences. It pools exact categorical answers with permissively scored numerical estimates, changes original benchmark protocols, and weights categories by sample count despite markedly unequal category sizes. Single-image models receive only the first frame of multi-image tasks, making some failures attributable to unavailable evidence. Format-specific chance baselines, threshold sensitivity, and separate reporting of unsupported inputs would make the conclusions more reliable.

The benchmark collection and tool integration have worthwhile value, but the unresolved answerability and evaluation confounds affect the central scientific claims, rather than merely presentation. These concerns determine the weak-reject recommendation despite the substantial experimental effort.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer vision problem: evaluating geometric capabilities that conventional semantic VQA benchmarks insufficiently test. VGBench contributes 6,000 questions covering camera parameters, pose, homography, depth, correspondence, and object location.

SpatialScore offers useful evaluation breadth: 28,093 samples from 12 sources, eight task categories, and multiple input and answer formats. Evaluating 25 open models, with detailed category and source breakdowns, provides a substantial empirical resource.

SpatialAgent demonstrates promising practical gains on SpatialScore-Hard. For example, InternVL3-8B improves from 12.86% to 46.08% with Plan-Execute, while Qwen2.5-VL-7B improves from 15.21% to 35.30%. These results support the usefulness of integrating specialist vision tools with language models.

The supplementary material provides extensive question templates, tool specifications, prompts, inference settings, and source statistics. The qualitative results also acknowledge failures, including confusing pixel distances with metric distances.
weaknesses: The central benchmark has unresolved answerability problems. Appendix D.2 asks for 3D boxes in world coordinates from an image without specifying the world-to-camera transformation. Such coordinates cannot generally be recovered from the supplied input. Figure 7 asks models to distinguish focal lengths of 792.59 and 792.95 pixels from a single ordinary image, without calibration information or an uncertainty allowance. These examples conflate geometric understanding with recovery of unavailable or insufficiently constrained information. No human evaluation establishes answerability, despite the introduction claiming a gap to humans.

Question construction and scoring impose inconsistent precision requirements. Distance distractors are generated within ±50% of the ground truth (Appendix D.2), so every such distractor would satisfy the factor-of-two correctness criterion used for open-ended distance answers. Consequently, nominally equivalent questions can require very different precision depending on format. Figure 2 also includes negative object-size distractors despite claims of physically plausible alternatives. There is no text-only baseline or quantitative distractor audit to establish how much accuracy reflects visual geometry rather than answer-option artifacts.

SpatialScore-Hard is selected specifically for failures by many of the same models subsequently ranked on it, including the agent backbones. This is legitimate for failure analysis, but their very low scores and the agent's recovery should not be interpreted as representative performance comparisons. SpatialAgent is evaluated quantitatively only on this selected subset; evaluation on the full benchmark or an independently selected subset is absent. The manual verification process also lacks annotator counts, agreement measurements, and a quantified ambiguity audit.

The agent experiments establish the benefit of the complete system but do not isolate the claimed contribution of multi-agent orchestration. Plan-Execute and ReAct are established approaches, and there are no tool-removal ablations, simpler tool-routing baselines, or matched-budget reasoning controls. Appendix D.3 gives ordinary models 512 output tokens while agents receive 2,048 tokens and multiple calls. Without latency, tool-use statistics, or compute-matched comparisons, the gains cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed orchestration.

Some broader conclusions exceed the evidence. Single-image models receive only the first frame of multi-image or video inputs, making their results partly a test of missing information; formatting failures also contribute to low scores of spatially fine-tuned models. These factors weaken the claim that such models generally lack spatial generalization. Overall, the dataset integration and tool-assisted results are worthwhile, but the unresolved validity of the new geometry benchmark and the confounded agent evaluation currently outweigh those merits.
